<STRUCT_0001>
In general it does not make sense to compose rational maps. The reason
is that the image of a representative of the first rational map may
have empty intersection with the domain of definition of the second.
However, if we assume that our schemes are irreducible and we look
at dominant rational maps, then we can compose rational maps.

Let <MATH_0001> and <MATH_0002> be irreducible schemes. A rational map from <MATH_0003> to <MATH_0004>
is called <TEXTITOPEN_0001>dominant<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> if any representative <MATH_0005> is a dominant
morphism of schemes.

<STRUCT_0001>
By Lemma <REF_0001>
it is equivalent to require that the generic point <MATH_0001>
maps to the generic point <MATH_0002> of <MATH_0003>, i.e., <MATH_0004> for
any representative <MATH_0005>. We can compose a dominant rational map
<MATH_0006> between irreducible schemes <MATH_0007> and <MATH_0008> with an arbitrary rational
map <MATH_0009> from <MATH_0010> to <MATH_0011>. Namely, choose
representatives <MATH_0012> with <MATH_0013> open dense
and <MATH_0014> with <MATH_0015> open dense. Then
<MATH_0016> is open nonempty (because it contains the
generic point of <MATH_0017>) and we let <MATH_0018> be the
equivalence class of <MATH_0019>. We omit the verification
that this is well defined.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
In this way we obtain a category whose objects are irreducible schemes
and whose morphisms are dominant rational maps. Given a base scheme
<MATH_0020> we can similarly define a category whose objects are irreducible schemes
over <MATH_0021> and whose morphisms are dominant <MATH_0022>-rational maps.
